title: Siyum
hookLine: a celebration for finishing, with food and gratitude
tomorrow: why does a king beg his guests to stay one more day?

lines: A BAKERY BOX, HELD LIKE A TORAH.
cards: Saba David comes through the kitchen door with a bakery box held out in front of him like a Torah. Inside, a chocolate cake, and in wobbly blue frosting: AVOT. DONE.
Last night, on the phone, he and Noa read the final saying of the text they've been learning all summer. Noa thinks a cake is a lot for one little book. Saba disagrees, and he has backup.

In the Talmud, a sage named Abaye says: may it be counted to my credit that whenever I saw a young scholar finish a tractate, I threw a celebration for the rabbis. Not for his own finish. For someone else's.

teach.b: That celebration has a name: a siyum, a completion. When someone finishes a tractate of Talmud, a book of the Bible, or an order of the Mishnah, people gather.
The finisher reads the last passage aloud. Then come the closing words, the promise to return that you've heard before. And then, always, food.

teach.h: THE MEAL IS PART OF THE MITZVAH.
teach.b: In Jewish law a meal like this counts as a seudat mitzvah, a feast that is itself a good deed. Not a reward after the holy part. Part of the holy part.
Here's the detail to tell someone tonight.
On the day before Passover, firstborn sons have a custom of fasting, and a custom grew up of holding a siyum that morning, so they can join the celebration meal and break the fast.
Learning, literally, puts food on the table. So taste is how this tradition marks a finish. Not a certificate, not a grade.
A cake on the kitchen counter, a few people who care, and someone, maybe not even the one who finished, saying this deserves a party.

how: When someone completes a tractate of Talmud or another major text, Jews hold a siyum: the finisher reads the last passage, the hadran is said, and a celebratory meal (seudat mitzvah) follows; a siyum is held on the morning before Passover for firstborns who would otherwise fast.

games.q: your aunt finishes a book of the Bible with her study group and plans to just quietly start the next one. you've heard of Abaye. what do you do?
o: bring something to eat and gather a few people; her finish deserves a party.
say nothing; celebrating would embarrass a serious learner.
wait until she's finished the whole Bible before celebrating anything.
games.why: Abaye threw celebrations when others finished a tractate. a siyum marks the finish with people and food, and anyone can make it happen.

practice: Find something small to eat or drink, anything you enjoy. Before tasting it, say out loud one thing you've finished lately, a book, a project, a hard week, these years of the path.
Then taste it slowly, and let it be a celebration, even a tiny one. If someone's near, give them a bite and tell them why.

wordCard.voice: Siyum: completion. The gathering when someone finishes a text, with its last words read aloud, and a meal that counts as a good deed.

orig.note: Hebrew: completion; the celebration for finishing a text.
